extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, mathematicians, and educated readers interested in Omar Khayyam's scientific work
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the mathematical contributions, methods, originality, and limitations of Omar Khayyam based on his surviving algebra and calendar work. The rubric emphasizes both technical achievements (classification of cubics, geometric solution methods) and scholarly qualities (systematic exposition, completeness, relation to predecessors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / relative greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of Omar's originality and whether that originality makes him the greatest among Saracen mathematicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states he is "inclined to think that Omar Khayyam was the most original and, therefore, the greatest of the Saracen mathematicians." Originality is treated as the chief merit when ranking historical mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on pure mathematics vs applied mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the mathematician works as a pure mathematician (theory for its own sake) or primarily in applied mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues there is but one mathematics (pure mathematics) and praises those who work in abstract areas (Gauss is cited as praising number theory for having no practical application). This criterion values theoretical depth over practical application when assessing greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution to algebra (scope and significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive contribution to the field of algebra, especially treating equations beyond the quadratic and classifying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar's "algebra" is called his only known mathematical work; his treatment of equations of degree higher than the second and his classification of cubics are cited as major advances. The author calls algebra "the 'soul' of modern mathematics," implying weight given to achievements in algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of cubic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the mathematician classifies cubic equations comprehensively and in a way that generalizes to higher degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar's "complete classification of the cubic equation" is described as his greatest original contribution; he distinguished trinomial from tetranomial cubics and formed subgroups based on missing terms or equality relations among terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution methods (geometric constructions vs algebraic calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods used to solve equations: use of geometric constructions (intersections of conic sections) versus algebraic/calculational solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar solved equations by intersecting conic sections and believed cubics could not be solved by calculation, accepting geometric construction as the appropriate mode. The text notes this as characteristic and consequential to his practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic exposition and use of lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and systematic structure of mathematical exposition, including prefacing sections with lemmas and organized proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises Omar as "very systematic throughout, prefacing each section by such lemmas as he will have to use," indicating that organized presentation and preparatory lemmas are valued in judging mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of demonstrations (geometrical style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The favored form of demonstration (e.g., geometric proofs) and whether this form is appropriate or limiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All Omar's demonstrations are "given in geometrical form, which was the standard form among the Greeks;" the essay notes this practice and links it to both tradition and to how algebraic ideas were represented (powers named from geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation and symbolic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (or lack) of symbolic notation in algebraic work and the implications for clarity and generality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Saracen algebraists, including Omar, used names rather than symbols (following Diophantos's practice). The essay contrasts this rhetorical notation with symbolic methods, implying that notation choice is a relevant evaluative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and attention to special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughness in considering exceptional or particular cases (e.g., existence of multiple positive roots, use of multiple branches of curves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes Omar for sometimes overlooking particular cases (failing to see that x^3 + bx = ax^2 + c may have three positive real roots) and for "lost many roots by using only one branch of a hyperbola," marking completeness as an important standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative rigor in parameter/coefficients analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision in investigating the numerical ranges of coefficients necessary to produce real intersections or solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar is said to have been "not very exact in the investigation of the numerical values that the several coefficients must have" for real intersections of conics; careful analysis of parameter conditions is implied as a criterion of rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of solvability limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness and correct assessment of which classes of equations are solvable by given methods (e.g., geometric construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar considered biquadratic equations unsolvable by geometric constructions. The essay treats correct identification of solvability boundaries as a legitimate feature of one's mathematical judgment (whether right or wrong).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic theorems (e.g., binomial theorem) and root-extraction methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment and extension of algebraic results such as the binomial theorem for positive integral exponents and methods for extracting higher roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar apparently considered the binomial theorem and said: "I have taught how to find the sides of the square-square, of the square-cube...to any extent," which the author interprets as use of such theorems for root extraction in the Hindoo manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of geometric construction problems to algebraic equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to translate geometric construction problems into algebraic equations and solve them (e.g., reducing a construction to x^4 + bx = ax^3 + c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omar solved a geometric problem (constructing an equilateral trapezoid with given base/side length and given area) by reducing it to the quartic x^4 + bx = ax^3 + c, showing skill in algebraic reduction of geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/astronomical contributions and numerical accuracy (calendar reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions to astronomy/chronology and the numerical precision of those contributions (e.g., calendar correction accuracy vs Gregorian reform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 1079 Omar corrected the calendar using 33-year cycles with 8 leap-years per cycle; his average year is computed as more accurate than the Gregorian by the small second differences cited. The author uses this numerical comparison as evidence of technical competence and practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to predecessors and transmission of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the mathematician builds on, translates, or diverges from predecessors (Diophantos, Al-Khwarizmi) and whether influence is acknowledged or detectable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay discusses traces of Diophantos's influence in Omar's algebra and notes that Saracen algebraists adopted Diophantos's names; establishing lines of influence and originality over predecessors is used to evaluate contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of surviving work and its representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the extant work (e.g., the algebra) is representative of the mathematician's capabilities and how much the surviving corpus limits assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes "the only mathematical work of Omar with which we are acquainted is his 'algebra'," which frames judgments: limited surviving material constrains evaluation of overall ability.
